points/tokens: A model computes with numbers, so text has to become numbers first. Cut it into tokens, the pieces the model reads: here, whole words.
points/vocab: The list of every token a model knows is its vocabulary. Number the list from zero, and each token's number is its id.
points/line: But an id is only a filing number. It puts car between cat and dog, as if a car were halfway from a cat to a dog, and says nothing about which words are alike.
points/points: So give each token a vector instead: two numbers here, a point on a plane. Put cat and dog close together, and car and bus together, off in another direction.
points/dot: Now the dot product says how alike two tokens are. Cat dot dog is three times three, plus one times two: eleven.
points/dot2: Cat dot car is minus three, plus three: zero. A right angle: nothing in common.
points/name: A token's vector is called its embedding: the token is embedded, set in place, as a point in a space where nearness means something.
points/firth: Why should nearness mean anything? In 1957, the linguist John Rupert Firth put it this way: you shall know a word by the company it keeps.
table/stack: Stack every token's vector as a row, in order of id, and you have the embedding table, E. Row zero is cat's point: three, one.
table/V: It has one row per token: V rows, V for the size of the vocabulary. Here V is four.
table/d: And one column per number in a vector: d columns, d for the embedding's size. Here d is two, so E is four by two.
table/lookup: To embed a token, read its row. Dog has id two, so its embedding is row two: three, two. That is the third row down, because ids count from zero.
table/count: The table holds V times d numbers: four times two, eight.
table/bengio: In 2003, Yoshua Bengio and three colleagues gave each word a row like this, learned from text, so that words used alike, such as cat and dog, could land near each other.
table/big: Their vocabularies held about seventeen thousand words, with up to a hundred numbers each: one point seven million numbers.
onehot/x: There is a second way to reach a row. Put a vector, x, on the left of E, with one entry per row: one, two, zero, zero.
onehot/col: x times E dots x with each column of E. Down the first: one times three, plus two times minus one, is one. The second column gives seven.
onehot/rows: Read it by rows instead, and it is one times row zero, plus two times row one. x times E weighs each row of E by its entry, and adds them up.
onehot/onehot: Now write dog's id, two, as a one-hot vector: all zeros except a one in place two. One entry is on, or hot, which gives it the name.
onehot/picks: Times E, it weighs every row by zero except row two, which it weighs by one. So one-hot times E is exactly row two: dog's embedding.
onehot/same: A lookup is a product with a one-hot vector. Reading the row directly gives the same answer, and skips every multiplication by zero.
batch/seq: Text comes as a sequence, tokens in order: dog, cat, bus, car is four ids, two, zero, three, one.
batch/rows: Look them all up at once, and every id becomes its row: four rows of two numbers, a shape of four by two.
batch/batch: Stack three such sequences, shape three by four, and the lookup gives three by four by two: the ids keep their shape, and gain a last axis of d numbers.
